o: We must XOR the value `((nums[i] | nums[j]) & nums[k])` over **all** $O(n^3)$ index triplets. In Example 1 the eight triplet values are `1,0,1,4,1,4,0,4`, whose XOR is `5`. Brute-forcing all triplets is impossible for $n \le 10^5$ ($10^{15}$ operations), so we need a mathematical shortcut. Since XOR acts independently on each bit, we can analyze one bit at a time and only track whether the total count of triplets setting that bit is odd or even.
k: XOR distributes bitwise: compute each bit position independently and only its parity matters.
For a fixed bit, if it appears in $c$ of the first-two-index values and $m$ times overall, the number of triplets setting it has parity $c \cdot m \bmod 2$.
The whole answer collapses to the XOR of all array elements.

a.i: Work bit by bit. For bit $b$, let $m$ be the number of elements having that bit and $c$ the number of elements having it (counted over the roles of indices $i$ and $j$, so effectively $2c$ slot-occurrences). A triplet sets the bit iff $(u_i \lor u_j) \land u_k = 1$. Summing over choices, the count of such triplets is $(\text{pairs with } u_i \lor u_j = 1) \times m$, whose parity equals $c \cdot m \bmod 2$ (each factor reduces to the count of ones modulo 2). So bit $b$ appears in the final XOR exactly when an odd number of elements contain bit $b$ — i.e., the answer is simply the XOR of all elements. This approach makes the reasoning explicit without needing the closed-form leap.
s: For each bit b from 0 to 30, count m = number of nums[i] with bit b set.
If m is odd, set bit b in ans.
a.t: O(31 · n) — one pass over the array per bit position.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only counters and the answer.

a.n: Approach 2: Direct XOR of All Elements (Optimal)
a.i: From the per-bit analysis, a bit ends up in the answer iff an odd number of elements contain it — which is precisely the definition of the XOR of the whole array. Hence the xor-beauty equals `nums[0] ^ nums[1] ^ ... ^ nums[n-1]`, computable in a single pass.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work per element.

w: In an interview, derive Approach 1 (bit-by-bit parity) to show reasoning, then present the one-line insight that the answer is just the XOR of all elements (Approach 2). Common pitfalls: attempting the $O(n^3)$ brute force (TLE for $n = 10^5$), mishandling the fact that $i$ and $j$ play symmetric roles while $k$ does not, and forgetting values fit in 31 bits so plain `int` suffices. Edge cases: single-element arrays (answer is that element) and duplicate values. Likely follow-ups: generalize to quadruplets or different operator combinations, or prove the identity formally using the ring structure of XOR/AND/OR.
